summary: Describes the Sun RPC version 2 message protocol that Sun Microsystems and others used for remote procedure calls, proposed for the Internet's consideration. It was not an Internet standard. It replaces RFC 1050.

plainLanguage.summary: Sun RPC lets a program send a request for a procedure to run on another machine and receive a reply. This RFC defines the message format and authentication fields, but leaves transport reliability and service binding to other mechanisms.

subtitle: How Sun RPC names remote procedures and formats calls, replies and authentication data.

tldr.problem: Programs on separate machines need a shared way to name a remote procedure, match its reply to the call and carry authentication information.
tldr.mechanism: RPC version 2 defines call and reply messages in XDR. Calls identify a program, version and procedure; replies report acceptance, results or an error.
tldr.outcome: The RFC describes a protocol used by Sun Microsystems and others and proposes it for Internet consideration. It is Informational, not an Internet standard, and obsoletes RFC 1050.

today: RFC 1057 is an Informational memo, not an Internet standard. It replaces RFC 1050.

sections.title: The Remote Procedure Call Model
sections.content:
RFC 1057 specifies version two of the message protocol used in Sun's Remote Procedure Call (RPC) package. A client sends a call containing parameters to a server, which sends a reply containing results. A program may support multiple versions so clients can use different versions of its service.

Unlike a local procedure call, a remote call can fail because of a server or network problem, cannot use the caller's global variables or side effects, and is slower. The protocol places no restriction on whether calls are synchronous or asynchronous. Binding a client to a service is outside this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A client asks a server to run a named procedure and waits for its reply. The network may fail, so programs must handle outcomes that cannot happen with a local call.

sections.title: RPC Calls and Replies
sections.content:
Every RPC message begins with a transaction identifier, xid, and a message type: CALL or REPLY. The reply carries the call's xid, which helps match replies to calls or recognize retransmissions; it is not a sequence number.

A call gives the RPC version, program number, program version and procedure number, followed by credentials, a verifier and procedure-specific parameters. Version two requires rpcvers to equal 2. A reply distinguishes accepted calls from denied calls and can report success, unavailable programs or procedures, version mismatch, bad arguments or authentication failure.
sections.plainLanguage: The call identifies the program and procedure and carries its arguments and authentication fields. The reply matches the call and reports either results or a reason the request could not be completed.

sections.title: Transport and Record Marking
sections.content:
RPC defines message meaning, not how messages travel, and it does not provide reliability. Over UDP, an application must provide its own timeouts, retransmission and duplicate detection. Over a reliable transport such as TCP, a reply can indicate execution, but a missing reply does not prove that the procedure did not run.

When RPC uses a byte stream, record marking separates messages. One RPC message forms one record, which may contain one or more fragments. Each fragment begins with a four-byte header: its highest-order bit marks the last fragment, and its remaining 31 bits give the fragment length in bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: RPC does not resend lost messages or decide whether a procedure ran more than once. When a byte stream carries RPC, a four-byte marker tells the receiver each fragment's size and whether it ends the record.

sections.title: Authentication and the Port Mapper
sections.content:
RPC call messages carry credentials and a verifier; replies carry a response verifier. The RPC layer treats their bodies as opaque and uses an authentication flavor to identify the separate mechanism. RFC 1057 describes AUTH_NULL, AUTH_UNIX, AUTH_SHORT and AUTH_DES. AUTH_UNIX sends machine and user information but has no real verifier; AUTH_DES uses a network name, encrypted timestamp and a conversation key.

The port mapper associates an RPC program, version and transport with a port number. Programs register mappings and clients ask for them; the port mapper uses port 111 and program number 100000 in this specification. It also supports broadcast calls by forwarding them to a local program over UDP.
sections.plainLanguage: RPC carries identity information, but separate authentication mechanisms define how to check it. A port mapper tells a client which transport port serves a particular program and version.
